title: Choosing a Data Model in Microsoft Fabric: Technique, Store, and Read Mode
purpose: Give a practitioner a branching decision path for three separable modelling choices in Fabric — the logical modelling technique (dimensional star schema vs data vault), the physical store that hosts it (Lakehouse vs Warehouse), and the semantic-model storage mode that reads it (Direct Lake vs Import vs DirectQuery/composite) — plus the one well-documented trap that silently forces a fallback.
accessibleSummary: A three-gate decision tree. Gate 1 asks what the model must optimise for: BI query simplicity branches to a dimensional star schema, while auditable history across many volatile sources branches to data vault — a trade-off panel notes vault is never queried directly by BI. Gate 2 asks which engine owns writes: Spark and multi-format engineering branches to a Lakehouse over managed Delta tables, T-SQL with multi-table transactions branches to a Warehouse, also Delta underneath — both converge on gate 3. Gate 3 asks how the semantic model should read the conformed table, per table rather than once for the model: Direct Lake for large, fresh facts with no import; Import for compact, fully modellable tables; DirectQuery or composite for source-authoritative or exception tables. A warning node, reached only from the Direct Lake branch, flags that basing a Direct Lake on SQL table on a SQL view forces every query into DirectQuery fallback — a sourced Microsoft documentation fact, not a hypothetical — and that fallback lands the query on the DirectQuery branch anyway.
longDescription: This diagram sequences three modelling decisions that Fabric practitioners often conflate into one choice. The first gate is purely logical: what must the model optimise for. A dimensional star schema (conformed dimensions plus grain-declared fact tables) is the default when the consumer is BI and query simplicity matters most; Fabric's own warehouse tutorial content backs a practical fact-table design heuristic here (a fact table carrying more than roughly 50 columns is usually hiding a dimension that should be split out). Data vault (hubs, links, satellites) is reserved for cases where auditable history across many volatile, frequently-changing source systems is the actual requirement — not a default, because it is never queried directly by BI and needs a dimensional layer built on top of it for reporting. The second gate is physical: which engine owns the writes. A recommended Fabric medallion pattern keeps Bronze/Silver in a Lakehouse for Spark-based ETL, while the Gold star-schema layer is built either as Lakehouse materialized views or as a Warehouse using T-SQL, with the Warehouse reading Lakehouse tables via cross-database queries — both stores persist Delta, so this gate is decided by engine and transaction needs, not storage format. The third gate is how the semantic model reads the conformed table, and it is decided per table, not once for the whole model: Direct Lake reads Delta columns directly from OneLake with no import refresh, and composite models let very large fact tables stay Direct Lake while smaller dimension tables use Import or DirectQuery in the same model. A warning branch, reached specifically from the Direct Lake path, documents a concrete, sourced trap: in Direct Lake on SQL, basing a model table on a SQL analytics-endpoint view rather than a base table forces every query against that table into DirectQuery fallback, which is documented as a real Microsoft-listed fallback trigger alongside row-level security on the SQL endpoint and Delta tables that exceed capacity guardrails — and the fallback edge routes that traffic onto the same DirectQuery/composite branch used deliberately elsewhere in the tree.

nodes.label: Gate 1 — What must the model optimise for?
nodes.summary: The root question: choose the modelling technique from the job the model has to do, not from habit.
nodes.detail: The first decision is purely logical, made before any physical engine is chosen. It asks what the model exists to optimise: fast, simple BI query patterns over a declared grain, or auditable history across many volatile source systems. Picking a technique from habit — always building a star schema, or always building a vault — skips the question this gate exists to force.
nodes.whyItMatters: Every downstream choice (physical store, semantic read mode) inherits the shape decided here; retrofitting a technique after physical build-out is expensive because the grain, keys, and history model are baked into the tables.

inputs: The consumer profile (BI analysts vs data engineers)
The history requirement (point-in-time reporting vs full audit trail vs current-state only)
The number and volatility of source systems feeding the entity
processing: Identify the dominant consumer and their query pattern
Determine whether auditable history is a genuine requirement or a nice-to-have
outputs: A chosen modelling technique (dimensional or data vault) with the reason recorded
drill.example: A finance reporting team needs fast, simple slice-and-dice over sales facts by date, product, and region — this is a straightforward vote for a dimensional star schema over data vault's extra join complexity.
controls: Explicit written rationale for the chosen technique, reviewed when the workload changes
Revisit trigger: a change in consumer profile or a new regulatory audit requirement
failureModes: Defaulting to data vault for a team that only ever needs current-state BI reporting, paying join complexity for history nobody queries
Defaulting to a star schema when many volatile upstream systems actually need auditable, replayable history

nodes.label: Dimensional / star schema
nodes.summary: Facts at a declared grain plus conformed dimensions — the default when BI query simplicity is the goal.
nodes.detail: A fact table records events or measurements at a single declared grain, joined to conformed dimension tables holding descriptive attributes. This is the classic Kimball pattern and remains the default choice inside Fabric Warehouses and Lakehouse gold layers when the dominant consumer is BI. A practical Fabric-sourced design heuristic: a fact table carrying more than roughly 50 columns is usually hiding attributes that belong in a dimension instead — a signal the grain or normalisation has drifted.
nodes.whyItMatters: Star schemas keep BI query patterns simple (single joins from fact to dimension, predictable aggregation paths) and are what Direct Lake and Import semantic models are optimised to read efficiently.

evidence.note: A practitioner heuristic: a fact table with more than roughly 50 columns is likely carrying attributes that should be split out into a dimension table instead.

inputs: Conformed business keys and measures identified during gate 1
A declared grain (one row per what, at what level of detail)
processing: Design fact table(s) at the declared grain with foreign keys to dimensions
Design conformed dimension tables shared across fact tables where the same entity recurs
Apply the >50-column heuristic to catch fact tables absorbing dimension attributes
outputs: A star (or snowflake) schema ready to host in a Lakehouse gold layer or Warehouse
drill.example: A sales fact table at the grain of one row per order line joins to Date, Product, Customer, and Store dimensions — a BI report slices revenue by any combination without touching source system tables directly.
controls: Grain declaration reviewed before build, not after
Column-count review against the ~50-column heuristic during design review
failureModes: Mixed-grain fact tables (some rows at order level, some at line level) silently double-counting aggregates
A fact table absorbing descriptive attributes instead of a dimension, bloating row size and breaking the >50-column heuristic

nodes.label: Data vault
nodes.summary: Hubs, links, satellites — used only when auditable history across many volatile sources is the actual requirement.
nodes.detail: Data vault decomposes an entity into a hub (business key), links (relationships between hubs), and satellites (descriptive attributes and history), insulating the model from source-system change and preserving a full audit trail. It is not queried directly by BI — a dimensional layer is still built on top of the vault for reporting, which is why this branch feeds back toward the same physical and semantic gates as the dimensional branch rather than skipping them.
nodes.whyItMatters: Vault earns its extra join complexity only when the audit and source-volatility requirement is real; used as a default it adds cost with no corresponding BI benefit, since reporting still needs a star schema built on top of it.

inputs: Business keys from multiple volatile source systems that need independent load and audit tracking
processing: Model each core business concept as a hub keyed on its business key
Model relationships between hubs as links
Attach descriptive, time-versioned attributes as satellites per source
outputs: An auditable, source-insulated vault layer, plus a dimensional layer built on top of it for BI consumption
drill.example: A customer entity fed by three regional CRM systems is modelled as one customer hub, with a satellite per source system capturing each system's version of the attributes over time — full audit trail preserved even as source systems change.
controls: Load pattern (batch vs incremental) per satellite
The dimensional layer built on top, since vault itself is never the BI-facing layer
failureModes: Reporting directly against vault tables instead of building the dimensional layer on top, exposing join complexity to BI users
Adopting vault for a single stable source system where the audit and insulation benefit never materialises

nodes.label: Gate 2 — Which engine owns the writes?
nodes.summary: Second question: Lakehouse or Warehouse, decided by engine and transaction needs, not by storage format.
nodes.detail: Both a Fabric Lakehouse and a Fabric Warehouse persist Delta tables, so choosing between them is not a storage-format decision. A recommended Fabric medallion pattern keeps Bronze and Silver in a Lakehouse for Spark-based ETL, CDC, and feature engineering, while the Gold star-schema layer is built either as Lakehouse materialized views or as a Warehouse with T-SQL, with the Warehouse reading Lakehouse tables via cross-database queries when the two are split.
nodes.whyItMatters: Picking the physical store by 'which one is newer' or 'which one I know' instead of by engine and transaction fit produces avoidable friction later — multi-table ACID transactions and a full T-SQL surface belong in a Warehouse; Spark-native transformation and mixed file/table workloads belong in a Lakehouse.

inputs: A modelling technique chosen at gate 1
The primary transformation engine skill in the team (Spark vs T-SQL)
Whether a load must commit atomically across multiple related tables
processing: Route Spark-native ETL, CDC, and feature-engineering workloads to a Lakehouse
Route multi-table ACID transactions and heavy T-SQL usage to a Warehouse
Allow a split medallion where Bronze/Silver sit in a Lakehouse and Gold is built as a Warehouse, joined via cross-database query
outputs: A chosen physical store (or a split Lakehouse/Warehouse medallion) hosting Delta tables
drill.example: A team runs Spark notebooks for Bronze-to-Silver conformance in a Lakehouse, then a Warehouse Gold layer holds the star schema with stored procedures and multi-table transactional loads, querying the Lakehouse's Silver tables cross-database.
controls: Team skill profile (Spark vs T-SQL) driving engine choice
Whether the workload needs multi-table transactional guarantees
failureModes: Building multi-table ACID logic in a Lakehouse via notebooks when a Warehouse would provide it natively
Splitting engines without a clear cross-database query contract, causing duplicated transformation logic

nodes.label: Lakehouse (Spark over managed Delta)
nodes.summary: Spark-native engineering over managed Delta tables — the Bronze/Silver home in the recommended medallion split.
nodes.detail: A Fabric Lakehouse stores managed Delta tables that Spark notebooks read and write natively, alongside an auto-provisioned SQL analytics endpoint for read access. In the medallion pattern this is documented as the recommended home for Bronze and Silver layers — Spark-based ETL, CDC, and feature engineering — with Gold optionally built here too as Lakehouse materialized views.
nodes.whyItMatters: Choosing Lakehouse commits the team to Spark as the primary transform engine for this layer; the SQL analytics endpoint is read-oriented, so multi-table transactional writes are not the Lakehouse's strength.

evidence.note: A recommended medallion pattern keeps Bronze and Silver layers in a Lakehouse for Spark-based ETL/CDC/feature engineering, while the Gold layer is built either as Lakehouse materialized views or as a Warehouse with T-SQL star schemas, with the Warehouse reading Lakehouse tables via cross-database queries.

inputs: A modelling technique and grain chosen upstream
Bronze/Silver conformance workloads authored as Spark notebooks or Dataflows Gen2
processing: Write and manage Delta tables in the Lakehouse Tables area from Spark
Expose the same tables read-only through the auto-provisioned SQL analytics endpoint
Optionally build Gold as materialized views over Silver in the same Lakehouse
outputs: Managed Delta tables queryable by Spark and the SQL analytics endpoint, feeding Warehouse cross-database queries or a semantic model
drill.example: A Bronze-to-Silver pipeline runs entirely as Spark notebooks against Lakehouse Delta tables, then a Gold materialized view aggregates Silver into a star schema without a separate Warehouse.
controls: Choice of Spark runtime and job scheduling for the ETL workload
Whether Gold stays in-Lakehouse (materialized views) or moves to a Warehouse
failureModes: Treating the SQL analytics endpoint as a general write target when it is read-oriented
Skipping materialized-view refresh scheduling, leaving Gold aggregates stale

nodes.label: Warehouse (T-SQL, multi-table ACID)
nodes.summary: Full T-SQL surface with multi-table transactions over Delta — the recommended home for a Gold star schema with procedural logic.
nodes.detail: A Fabric Warehouse offers a full T-SQL surface — stored procedures, multi-table transactions — while still persisting data as open Delta tables in OneLake underneath. The medallion pattern documents this as an alternative Gold-layer home to Lakehouse materialized views, reading upstream Bronze/Silver Lakehouse tables via cross-database queries.
nodes.whyItMatters: Choosing Warehouse commits to T-SQL as the Gold transformation language and gains multi-table ACID guarantees a Lakehouse notebook pipeline would have to build manually.

evidence.note: A recommended medallion pattern keeps Bronze and Silver layers in a Lakehouse for Spark-based ETL/CDC/feature engineering, while the Gold layer is built either as Lakehouse materialized views or as a Warehouse with T-SQL star schemas, with the Warehouse reading Lakehouse tables via cross-database queries.

inputs: Conformed Silver tables from an upstream Lakehouse, read via cross-database query
A star schema design from gate 1
processing: Load fact and dimension tables using T-SQL stored procedures with multi-table transactional guarantees
Apply the >50-column fact-table heuristic during design review
outputs: A Warehouse-hosted star schema, still Delta underneath, readable by any Fabric engine or a semantic model
drill.example: A nightly stored procedure loads the Gold fact and dimension tables inside a single transaction, guaranteeing the fact table and its dimensions are never left partially updated if the load fails midway.
controls: Stored procedure design for atomic multi-table loads
Cross-database query contract with the upstream Lakehouse Silver layer
failureModes: Cross-database query performance degrading if the Lakehouse-side tables are not compacted (small-file bloat)
Autonomous engine tuning behaving differently than expected under unusually skewed data distributions

nodes.label: Gate 3 — How should the semantic model read it?
nodes.summary: Third question, decided per table: Direct Lake, Import, or DirectQuery/composite.
nodes.detail: Once a table is physically built, the semantic model layer decides how to read it — and Fabric explicitly supports deciding this per table rather than once for the whole model. Composite models let very large fact tables stay in Direct Lake mode, avoiding scheduled refresh cost, while smaller dimension tables use Import or DirectQuery in the same model.
nodes.whyItMatters: Treating storage mode as a single whole-model setting forces a worse trade-off than necessary; deciding per table lets large fact tables avoid import cost while small dimension tables get full Import modelling flexibility.

evidence.note: Direct Lake on OneLake supports composite models, so very large fact tables can stay in Direct Lake mode (avoiding refresh cost) while dimension tables use Import or DirectQuery in the same model.

inputs: A physically built star schema or vault-derived dimensional layer in a Lakehouse or Warehouse
processing: Evaluate each table's freshness requirement, size, and required modelling features
Assign Direct Lake, Import, or DirectQuery per table rather than one mode for the whole model
Combine modes in a composite model where table needs differ
outputs: A semantic model with a storage mode assigned per table, balancing freshness, scale, and modelling flexibility
drill.example: A large sales fact table stays Direct Lake for near-real-time queries with no refresh job, while a small, curated currency-conversion dimension uses Import so calculated columns and complex M transformations are available on it.
controls: Per-table storage-mode assignment reviewed against freshness and modelling-feature needs
Composite-model design when table needs genuinely differ
failureModes: Applying one storage mode to the whole model instead of deciding per table, over-paying for import refresh on tables that didn't need it
Choosing Direct Lake for a table that needs Import-only modelling features (complex calculated columns, certain M transforms)

nodes.label: Direct Lake
nodes.summary: Delta columns read directly from OneLake — best fit for large, fresh fact tables with no import refresh.
nodes.detail: Direct Lake reads Delta table columns directly from OneLake without a separate import copy, so there is no scheduled refresh cost and the model reflects the underlying table as soon as it commits. It comes in two flavors: Direct Lake on OneLake (OneLake security, richer modelling features, faster queries) and Direct Lake on SQL (used when SQL analytics-endpoint security rules under delegated identity are needed, or when DirectQuery fallback behaviour is specifically required).
nodes.whyItMatters: Direct Lake is what makes very large fact tables viable in a semantic model without paying an import refresh window — but it is not unconditional, which is why the fallback trap sits directly on this branch.

evidence.note: Direct Lake comes in two storage-mode flavors: Direct Lake on OneLake (OneLake security, richer modeling features, faster queries) and Direct Lake on SQL (needed for SQL-endpoint security rules under delegated identity, or when DirectQuery fallback is required).

inputs: A conformed Delta table (base table, not a view) in a Lakehouse or Warehouse
processing: Model reads Delta Parquet columns directly from OneLake at query time
No scheduled import/refresh job runs for this table
Flavor chosen: OneLake connector for richer modelling and OneLake security, or SQL connector when SQL-endpoint security/fallback is specifically needed
outputs: Near-real-time query results reflecting the latest committed Delta version, with no refresh-staleness window
drill.example: A sales fact table updated hourly by a pipeline is read via Direct Lake on OneLake; a report opened five minutes after a load reflects the new data with no refresh job to wait on.
controls: Choice of Direct Lake on OneLake vs on SQL, identifiable from the model's M expression connector in TMDL view
Whether the base table (not a view) is what the model table maps to
failureModes: Basing a Direct Lake on SQL table on a view instead of a base table — see the linked warning node
Row/column cardinality exceeding capacity (F-SKU) guardrails, silently triggering fallback

nodes.label: Import
nodes.summary: Copied into semantic-model memory — best fit for compact, fully-modellable tables.
nodes.detail: Import mode copies data into the semantic model's in-memory store on a scheduled refresh, giving full modelling flexibility (calculated columns, the widest range of M transformations) at the cost of refresh latency and refresh-window operational overhead. It remains the right choice for small, curated, or heavily-transformed dimension tables even in an otherwise Direct-Lake-dominant composite model.
nodes.whyItMatters: Import is not obsolete under Direct Lake — composite models deliberately keep smaller dimension tables on Import specifically because they need modelling features Direct Lake tables don't get.

inputs: A compact dimension table or a table requiring calculated columns / complex M transforms
processing: Scheduled refresh copies the table into semantic-model memory
Full DAX calculated-column and M-transformation feature set is available on the copy
outputs: A fully-modellable in-memory table, refreshed on a defined schedule
drill.example: A currency-conversion dimension needs a calculated column blending two source rates; it stays Import in an otherwise Direct-Lake-dominant composite model so that calculated column is available.
controls: Refresh schedule and window
Monitoring for refresh failures causing silent staleness
failureModes: A missed or failed refresh going unnoticed, serving stale data with no visible error
Importing a table large enough that refresh time itself becomes the bottleneck

nodes.label: DirectQuery / composite
nodes.summary: Forwards queries to the source, or mixes modes per table — best fit for source-authoritative or exception tables.
nodes.detail: DirectQuery forwards each query to the underlying source at query time instead of reading a local copy, trading query-time source latency for always-current results and no refresh window. A composite model deliberately mixes DirectQuery, Import, and Direct Lake tables in the same model — the pattern Fabric documents for very large Direct Lake fact tables paired with Import or DirectQuery dimensions. This node also receives traffic involuntarily: a table that experiences DirectQuery fallback from the Direct Lake branch lands here too.
nodes.whyItMatters: This branch is both the deliberate exception path (tables that must stay source-authoritative) and the landing point for an unplanned Direct Lake fallback — which is why distinguishing a chosen DirectQuery table from a silently-fallen-back one matters operationally.

inputs: A table that must remain source-authoritative, or a table that has fallen back from Direct Lake
processing: Query forwarded to the source at query time rather than served from a local copy
In a composite model, mixed alongside Direct Lake and/or Import tables
outputs: Always-current query results at the cost of per-query source latency
drill.example: A composite model keeps a large sales fact table on Direct Lake while a slowly-changing regional-hierarchy dimension is deliberately left on DirectQuery against its source system of record.
controls: Deliberate per-table choice of DirectQuery vs relying on fallback
Query-time latency budget for DirectQuery tables
failureModes: Arriving at DirectQuery via an unplanned fallback rather than a deliberate choice — see the warning node
Query-time source latency compounding across multiple DirectQuery tables in one report

nodes.label: Trap: SQL view forces DirectQuery fallback
nodes.summary: In Direct Lake on SQL, a table based on a SQL view sends every query into DirectQuery fallback.
nodes.detail: Microsoft documents that basing a Direct Lake on SQL model table on a SQL analytics-endpoint view — rather than a base table — forces every query against that table into DirectQuery fallback, which usually slows it down. DirectQuery fallback exists only in Direct Lake on SQL, and its documented triggers are: querying a SQL-endpoint view, querying a table with SQL-endpoint row-level security, and a Delta table exceeding capacity guardrails. The recommended fix for a view-caused fallback is to materialize the view and remove non-deterministic functions from its definition.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is a silent trap: the model still returns correct results, so the fallback is invisible until someone investigates unexpectedly slow queries on a table that was supposed to be Direct Lake — exactly the kind of defect this diagram exists to make visible before it happens in production.

evidence.note: Basing a Direct Lake on SQL model table on a SQL view forces every query against that table into DirectQuery fallback, which usually slows it down; prefer base tables for Direct Lake mode.

inputs: A Direct Lake on SQL model table mapped to a SQL analytics-endpoint view instead of a base table
processing: Every query against that table is silently routed to DirectQuery fallback instead of the Direct Lake path
No error surfaces — only degraded query latency
outputs: Correct query results, delivered materially slower than the Direct Lake path the team believed was in use
drill.example: A team builds a Direct Lake on SQL table against a filtered SQL view meant to simplify the model; every report query against it silently falls back to DirectQuery, and the slowdown is only diagnosed weeks later using the community Semantic Link Labs library to check Direct Lake guardrails.
controls: Map Direct Lake on SQL tables to base tables, never views
If a view-shaped transformation is required, materialize it into a physical table and remove non-deterministic functions from its definition
Use a guardrail-checking tool to confirm which tables are actually resolving to Direct Lake vs silently falling back
failureModes: View-based table silently degrading to DirectQuery fallback with no visible error
Row-level security on the SQL endpoint or a table exceeding capacity guardrails triggering the same silent fallback via a different documented trigger

conformed Delta table ready for a semantic model

walkthrough.title: Start with what the model must optimise for
walkthrough.explanation: The root question is logical, not physical: what does this model need to be good at — BI simplicity or auditable history.

walkthrough.title: Branch: dimensional star schema
walkthrough.explanation: The default when BI query simplicity wins — facts at a declared grain joined to conformed dimensions, with a >50-column fact-table heuristic as a design smell test.

walkthrough.title: Branch: data vault
walkthrough.explanation: Reserved for genuine auditable-history-across-volatile-sources requirements — never queried directly by BI, so a dimensional layer still gets built on top.

walkthrough.title: Gate 2: which engine owns the writes
walkthrough.explanation: Both Lakehouse and Warehouse persist Delta — the decision is Spark vs T-SQL and whether multi-table ACID transactions are required, following the recommended medallion split.

walkthrough.title: Branch: Lakehouse over managed Delta
walkthrough.explanation: The recommended home for Spark-based Bronze/Silver ETL, with Gold optionally built here as materialized views.

walkthrough.title: Branch: Warehouse, T-SQL over Delta
walkthrough.explanation: The recommended home for a Gold star schema needing multi-table ACID transactions and a full T-SQL surface, reading Lakehouse Silver via cross-database query.

walkthrough.title: Gate 3: how the semantic model reads it, per table
walkthrough.explanation: Fabric composite models let this be a per-table decision — large fact tables can stay Direct Lake while other tables use Import or DirectQuery in the same model.

walkthrough.title: Branch: Direct Lake
walkthrough.explanation: Reads Delta columns straight from OneLake with no import refresh — the right fit for large, fresh fact tables, in either the OneLake or SQL flavor.

walkthrough.title: Warning: the SQL-view fallback trap
walkthrough.explanation: A documented, silent failure mode reached specifically from the Direct Lake branch: basing a Direct Lake on SQL table on a view instead of a base table forces every query into DirectQuery fallback with no visible error.

walkthrough.title: Branch: Import
walkthrough.explanation: Still the right choice for compact tables needing full modelling flexibility — calculated columns and complex M transforms that Direct Lake tables don't get.

walkthrough.title: Branch: DirectQuery / composite
walkthrough.explanation: The deliberate exception path for source-authoritative tables — and also where a silent fallback from the warning node lands, which is why the two connect.
